item.title: Connecting with Britain’s unsung carers has allowed me to feel a deep compassion for my younger self | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear and touching narrative

As the years have passed, I have often observed that caring for another person is a responsibility that few human beings completely escape. “Hardly anyone gets off scot-free in this life,” I recently said to a friend, as we discussed our various loved ones and their care needs, the worry and the responsibilities. Whether it’s our children, siblings, friends or parents, some sort of care work is usually required of us on our life’s journey. Illness, disability, mental health issues, ageing, accidents and other vulnerabilities inevitably touch our lives.

There are 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK, but I suspect there are far more who don’t identify as such, yet regularly care for loved ones or neighbours by helping with bills, shopping, appointments or more personal tasks. If you stood in a busy street in any town or city and stopped a passerby to ask them about the care they’ve given, or indeed the care they have received, many people would have a story to tell.

As someone who was a child carer for my profoundly autistic brother, this thought – that caring is something that unites us as human beings – is one I find comforting. This unspoken, hidden and often unwritten club is one that took me a long time to realise existed, simply because when you are little, most of your peers aren’t doing care work yet (and the ones who are might not talk about it). You also don’t necessarily see it as care because to you the tasks just feel normal: making their tea or helping them go to the toilet is simply a part of loving that person. Yet, having that level of responsibility as a child can feel very lonely, because you are a child with adult responsibilities who has had to grow up far too quickly. At the time you don’t realise that getting older means the size of this “club” keeps expanding. Now I am in my 30s and, having seen what life has thrown at the people I know and love, and their families, I understand that caring is less exceptional than it used to feel.

I recently contributed to an anthology for supporters of the Carers Trust called Lives Less Seen: Untold Stories from Those Who Care. Among the contributions are several from young carers. Oliver writes about looking after his mum, who had a stroke four years ago, and how being put in touch with the trust’s young carers network and campaigning politically for the rights of children like him has made him feel not only less alone but proud to be a young carer. Like the all-party parliamentary group that Oliver has attended, I’d like to see improved attempts to identify young carers, whose education, wellbeing and future prospects are all impacted by their roles, and better, earlier support for them, including when they transition to adulthood.

Caring is so often thankless, and its role in keeping society afloat is so often underestimated, that learning to feel pride in it is crucial.

The anthology also contains moving drawings from the Honeypot Children’s Charity, which supports young carers and children aged five to 12. Being put in touch with other child carers and being encouraged to creatively process their feelings must make such a difference. I rejected groups like these when I was young, I think from a mixture of pride and fear. In retrospect I think such initiatives would have really helped me make sense of what my home life involved. For a long time, I was so allergic to the idea that people may feel sorry for me that I had emotionally blocked off the possibility of ever feeling compassion for myself. I think a lot of carers do this, especially when they are in survival mode. It’s very easy to view being sad about it as something self-indulgent and unproductive, especially when you feel you’re not suffering anywhere near as much as the person you’re caring for, and so it’s easier to put your feelings in a box.

My own contribution to the anthology is a letter to my younger self, but really it is for all child carers. I wanted someone in my position to know how much I regretted not seeking support at the time. “There is great comfort to be had in community and solidarity,” I write. “Other people save us. Dealing with family illness or disability can be so hard, but the compensation is that often, along the way, you get to meet some of the best people ever.”

Caring is one of the hardest and one of the most life-affirming things I have done with my time on this planet. Unpaid carers might feel unseen, unappreciated and ignored by successive governments, but I do think those of us who care or who have cared share a common compassion, understanding and sense of humour that can be immensely comforting when it’s tapped into. That, at least, is something to be celebrated as we continue to campaign for better lives for all carers.

- Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist

Source: The Guardian Opinion | Published: 2026-11-23 06:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Undoing Brexit is the right thing to attempt – but sadly, I can't see Andy Burnham pulling it off | Paul Taylor
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, insightful analysis

Despite the beaming smiles and the symbolic triple handshake, the summit intended to reset the UK’s tortured relationship with the EU showed just how difficult undoing Brexit will be a decade after Britons voted to leave.

Andy Burnham’s first summit with the heads of the EU institutions felt like the homecoming of an old friend who had been away too long, rather than a meeting to settle some awkward leftovers of a bitter divorce.

There was positive progress on food and drink trade, youth mobility and aligning carbon markets. Yet there was also an inability to resolve relatively simple issues such as the fees young Europeans will pay to study at British universities from 2030, and whether the UK will apply the same tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as the EU. That is a taste of what lies ahead if a future government, backed by a groundswell of public opinion, decides to apply to rejoin.

The fundamental problems of being outside the EU were laid bare: you have to pay for market access and align with rules on which you no longer have a vote. But the issues around seeking renewed membership were also highlighted: the EU always has the upper hand in accession negotiations and the candidate country must adopt its rulebook wholesale – including the free movement of people – and pay into the common budget.

Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, was right to say the door is always open but at a price. Burnham is right to argue that Brexit has not benefited the economy, ordinary people or the UK’s standing in the world. However you do the counterfactual economics, Britain has lost substantial investment, export markets and potential growth, while citizens have faced increasing hassle travelling and living on both sides of the Channel. Young people have also been robbed of opportunities to study and work abroad. As the EU’s divorce negotiator, Michel Barnier, accurately forecast, Brexit has been a lose-lose equation for both sides.

However, the summit also illustrated that the toxic British politics around any move to rejoin have not gone away. Once again, the issue would dominate the agenda if the choice were put to a referendum or made the centrepiece of the next general election.

Burnham is correct to reopen a national debate on the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU and to put the option of membership back on the table. As ever, there is a domestic political calculation in his gamble. It helps Labour win back voters lost to the Greens and the Liberal Democrats in this year’s local elections and to mobilise pro-European youth support. He may also reckon that working-class voters lost to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK care more about cost of living issues than they do about Europe.

Farage, who built his career on stoking English nationalism and conflating EU membership with uncontrolled immigration, was quick to warn of a betrayal of the British people’s democratic 2016 vote by political elites. The line of the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, that Burnham had been made to accept an unfair deal, in which the UK will have to pay too much for too little return, was a telling indicator of the epic battles over money that lie ahead.

Signals from Brussels before the summit suggested the EU would probably not insist that the UK join the euro or the Schengen area of passport-free travel. But it was equally clear that Margaret Thatcher’s EU budget rebate, won after an epic battle in 1984, would not be returning.

It’s not clear that the UK’s political class or its powerful Treasury mandarins have accepted the fundamental pay-to-play logic of either partial access to the EU market or full membership. The widely held denial that Britain needs to pay for market access led to the collapse of negotiations last year to join the EU’s Security Action for Europe programme of soft loans for joint defence projects. Brussels shares responsibility for that failure by pitching an unrealistically high entry fee.

While many EU countries would welcome the UK back for geopolitical as well as economic reasons, especially in northern and central Europe, it is less clear that France, which since the presidency of Charles de Gaulle has seen Britain as aligned with US interests, would be so keen. If the hard-right nationalist Marine Le Pen, who applauded Brexit, wins next year’s French presidential election, she has vowed to reduce Paris’s contribution to EU coffers and may want to charge London a high price.

The prospect of an EU in which hard-right national populists, less supportive of Ukraine and more friendly in some cases towards Russia, enjoy growing influence may also make rejoining less politically attractive to a UK that is trying to shake off a decade of its own national populism.

I would love to see the UK back in the EU, where it always belonged as a European nation. But I’m not sure I will see it in my lifetime.

- Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre

Source: The Guardian Opinion | Published: 2026-11-23 05:00 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: Army’s plan to blow up aging explosives in Iowa will spread lead for miles – here’s what you need to know about the risks
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear explanation of risks

The U.S. Army set off waves of anxiety in Iowa in mid-November when it confirmed plans to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition plant, explosions that are expected to send a plume of lead particles – a neurotoxin – over homes and farmland for miles. Late on Nov. 22, 2026, the Army announced the rescheduled date: Nov. 25, the day before Thanksgiving.

According to the Army, dozens of old barrels containing lead azide, an explosive used as a detonator, have become unstable and pose an “unacceptable risk of accidental detonation” at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. Intentionally detonating the barrels is the best option for controlling the risk, the Army determined.

In Middletown, a community of about 360 residents in southeast Iowa, news reports described people taping windows to prepare for the blast and covering air conditioners with tarps to keep lead out. Communities and state politicians didn’t learn about the plan until a few days before Nov. 20, when the detonations were initially planned. A federal court paused the Army’s emergency Environmental Protection Agency permit after two groups sued, but the U.S. Justice Department argued that the permit wasn’t necessary in the face of an immediate threat.

To better understand the risks, we asked Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, what people in the region would face. O'Shaughnessy is part of a team scrambling to have testing in place when the Army carries out its detonation plan.

What risks do the Army’s planned explosions pose for people?

If you picture a dust plume, it carries particulate matter that can get into the lungs as you breathe. In this case, we’re talking about small particles that contain lead, which is toxic to humans and pets.

Those particles will settle over the area downwind of the detonation site. First it’s air pollution – if you’re outside, you can inhale those particles. Then it becomes surface pollution. The lead dust can get on your hands and into your body. The big concern there is for young children. If you think about 2-year-olds, they put everything in their mouths.

Lead is easily absorbed by the body. It gets into the bloodstream, and it can cause harm to just about every major organ in our bodies, including the nervous system and the brain. It tends to hide out in bones and teeth, where it can leach out and cause harm.

Studies have shown lead exposure is a major concern for pregnant women with developing fetuses. In young children, lead exposure can slow their brain development. Long-standing results from studies have demonstrated a reduction in IQ in children with chronic lead exposure, such as from lead-based paint in old houses.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there is no safe level of lead in the body. That’s a pretty strong statement.

What’s known about where the plume is likely to travel?

Where this plume travels and how far depends primarily on the wind speed and direction in the hours after the explosions.

We have a sense of what happens from studying pollution from smokestacks. Smokestacks are tall for a reason – they eject the pollutants high into the atmosphere so the pollutants dilute as they drift downwind.

In this case, instead of a steady stream coming out of the smokestack, it’s going to be a big puff that will literally create a cloud. That cloud will rise and start dissipating as it is diluted in the air. It will become invisible at some point, but that doesn’t mean the lead isn’t there.

If the Army had blown up those storage containers on Nov. 20, as initially planned, the forecast was for a fairly strong 15-mile-per-hour surface wind. The plume would have mostly diluted by the time it reached I-80, which is where I’m sitting, about 80 miles to the north.

If the Army goes through with its rescheduled plan, the preliminary forecast is for much slower wind blowing toward the south-southwest. Slower wind means the plume would affect a smaller area, but people there would experience a higher concentration of lead.

That may mean fewer people are affected, but the exposure could be more intense. We won’t know exactly what people will experience until it happens.

What can people do to stay safe in those areas?

Honestly, I would find a way to get out of the area for the day. If you can’t leave, the Army has a list of precautions that people should take, and I think those are good recommendations.

The Army is advising people near the plant to vacate their homes during the detonation and others to shelter in place. That means staying indoors and closing all your doors and windows. If you can, shut off the furnace – it pulls in air that could be contaminated as the plume travels through an area.

Within a few hours, the plume will have dissipated or moved on. But that doesn’t mean the lead disappears. It falls to the ground, meaning you and your pets can still get it on you.

After the plumed dissipates, the Army suggests getting a hose and spraying down window sills, cars, any horizontal surfaces where the dust can accumulate. Car door handles can easily collect and transfer the lead to people. If you have children’s play areas or toys outside, wash those down.

Lead is a persistent compound – there’s no way to degrade it. Washing it off surfaces transfers the lead to the soil. At this point in the year, the majority of the crops have been harvested, so there’s less risk of lead settling on plants in farm fields. However, some dairy farmers are concerned about their cows getting into lead that settles on grass.

Our results from sampling during and after the plume should help people better understand the risks.

What is your team planning for testing?…

In this stunning portrait, the Montreal-based filmmaker and photographer Sarah Seené captures the world of her friend Marie-Christine Ricignuolo, who lost most of her sight to congenital glaucoma several years ago at the age of 30. A comedian and actress who also tours as a public speaker, Ricignuolo reflects thoughtfully on her relationships with her partner, her son and the world she now interacts with quite differently – through memories, her limited sight and, above all, touch. Seené translates that sensory experience through analogue film, which she reworks with experimental processes to produce footage that is textured and ethereal, where even mundane events like a visit to the optician take on a strange beauty. The result is at once moving and inspiring, showing how, with the loss of even one of our most important senses, our capacity to find beauty in the world needn’t diminish, but can evolve and even be enriched.

item.title: Believing and thinking
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, thought-provoking analysis

Listen to this essay

26 minute listen

The idea of separating church and state – now entrenched in many modern liberal democracies – is in some ways strange. After all, governments must keep themselves informed and inform their citizens. That’s why they turn to the science of meteorology to predict weather patterns, to economics to understand patterns of growth and decline, and to the medical sciences to improve public health. So why wouldn’t governments also keep close alliances with religious institutions to know what’s going on with God?

Separating church and state appears strange from other perspectives as well. In the historical sweep of large-scale human societies, it’s a relative newcomer, often associated with the United States’ founding father Thomas Jefferson. In 1802, Jefferson asserted the principle of separation in a letter to the Danbury Baptist Association in Connecticut:

Believing with you that religion is a matter which lies solely between man and his God … that the legitimate powers of government reach actions only, and not opinions, I contemplate with sovereign reverence that act of the whole American people which declared that their legislature would ‘make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof,’ thus building a wall of separation between Church and State.

We’re fans of Jefferson’s principle, one of us (Neil Van Leeuwen) being a philosophy professor who grew up in the Christian Reformed Church, and the other (Jacob Eisler) being a law professor who regularly attends synagogue. But Jefferson’s letter makes putting the principle into practice sound simpler than it is – as though governments could be entirely hands-off when it comes to people’s beliefs, or ‘opinions’. That, however, can’t be right: engaging with and shaping political, social and other kinds of beliefs is actually a core function of government. Public education guides what people believe about everything from mathematics to history to astronomy. Governments also shape beliefs for policy reasons. If fire department officials learn that people believe a building is safe when it isn’t, they will try to change what people believe about the building’s safety. Belief is also a category of legal interest. If a psychotherapist, for example, believes a patient is a danger to himself or others, the therapist is obligated by law to report that belief.

All this means that Jefferson’s ‘wall of separation’ can’t sensibly prohibit governments from intervening on beliefs of any type whatsoever. Rather, Jefferson – along with advocates of the principle who came after him – must have presupposed that there is something distinctive about religious beliefs that makes it reasonable to give them a different legal status.

But what is this distinctive thing? Is it that religious beliefs concern God? No, because Buddhism is a religion with its own beliefs, yet Buddhism has no supreme deity. Is it that religious beliefs concern the supernatural generally? No, because many superstitions that aren’t part of a religion concern the supernatural too. Is it that religious beliefs concern morality, as the biologist Stephen Jay Gould once suggested? No, because many religious beliefs aren’t about morality, and many moral beliefs aren’t religious. In any case, any system of government must presuppose some moral beliefs – eg, that murder is wrong – to be a government at all. These considerations might make one despair of articulating the psychological distinction of interest – what’s different about religious ‘belief’? – that’s needed to make sense of separating church and state in the first place.

Such attempts at characterising religious belief fail, we think, because they focus on belief contents, or what the believing is about. But since any given idea can be believed in a religious way or not, that won’t work. Our suggestion, then, is that religiously believing is a different attitude from ordinary matter-of-fact believing – a different way of relating to ideas – and that this is what’s distinctive about religious belief. In other words, sacralising an idea is different from just taking it to describe how things are. Furthermore, empirical research in cognitive science and anthropology of religion, along with accompanying philosophical analysis, can help reveal characteristic features of the difference in attitude we’re after. To have specific terms, we call that the difference between religious credence and factual belief. Understanding this difference, we’ll see, helps make sense of Jefferson’s wall of separation, and supports the rationale for separating church and state in liberal democracies more generally.

Whatever they are, ‘beliefs’ come in different varieties. The word ‘belief’ is polysemous – meaning it can refer to a range of different-but-related things – and it subsumes a motley crew: from humdrum factual beliefs (say, about where the ice-cream store is) to superstitions (like those found in astrology), and from moral beliefs about murder to philosophical beliefs about how ‘all is one’. As mentioned earlier, beliefs can also be categorised by their contents (what is the belief about? Is it about politics? Or maybe about a probable scientific theory?) Or by the attitude they embody (how does a person relate to given ideas or contents?) Here, however, we focus on the differences between matter-of-fact believing and religious credence as distinct ways in which people process ideas. There are, of course, more varieties of belief-like attitudes. But we home in on factual belief and religious credence since the differences in those attitudes matter most to the psychology of separating church and state.…

item.title: Jo Marchant: In search of now
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, complex topic explained well

The meaning of ‘now’ might seem rather obvious: it’s the state of awareness you’re experiencing at this very moment, of course. But as the UK science writer Jo Marchant details in this talk at the Royal Institution in London, when you dig into how different disciplines and cultures understand the ‘now’, it gets rather knotty. Borrowing from research for her book In Search of Now (2026), Marchant traverses philosophy, physics, psychology and anthropology, deconstructing the concept to show why the present is so hard to pin down. She then ends on a practical note, weaving the mystery of ‘now’ into an argument for stepping out of clock time and tuning in to your experience.

item.title: How China became rich
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, informative on China's economic growth

This is our fourth article from Issue 26, which arrives with print subscribers this week.

Imagine if Y Combinator owned and ran San Francisco. Too much traffic? That’s bad for business. Highway 101 would be triple- or quadruple-deckered, and the metropolitan area might have a dozen subway lines, more like Madrid’s or Osaka’s networks than the BART as it stands. Heritage buildings? They’re nice, but this is a tech town. Skyscrapers would fill the entire peninsula. Instead of wealth taxes on billionaires, the city might even cut taxes to encourage more founders and companies to move there.

This is only a slight caricature of how city government works in China. Provincial cities like Hefei and Hangzhou have become world-leading centers of commerce in electric vehicles, consumer electronics, solar panels, batteries, and AI, steered by mayors whose career incentives are similar to those of partners in a venture capital firm, getting promoted if their portfolio grows and fired if it fails. The cities they run function as vertically integrated conglomerates that benefit not just from the success of their local champions, but also from the broader growth generated by masses of companies in their slipstream.

In the West, China’s success is often attributed to the central government’s willingness to pick winners and direct its economy from above. Many Westerners have concluded that a similar top-down approach is needed in their countries to create champions that can compete with China’s. But Beijing’s role is more akin to being a rulemaker in a great tournament. Subnational governments – provinces, cities, towns, villages – are responsible for around 85 percent of public expenditure, according to the IMF, the lion’s share of which is spent at city level.

The heavy state involvement correctly perceived by observers belongs not to Beijing but to those local governments, of which China has thousands, and which compete with one another for investment and prestige. These local growth machines and the competition between them are what drives China’s stunning economic success, and what the Western world must embrace to keep up.

Local heroes

For the initial decades after China’s economic opening in the 1980s, ‘Made in China’ meant cheap goods mass-produced for Western businesses. Today, Chinese companies lead the world in high-tech manufacturing, and many of them are household names in the West. Huawei is arguably the world’s most advanced telecoms company; BYD is the largest electric automaker; and DJI makes over 90 percent of consumer drones. Less familiar but no less important are companies like Geely, an auto giant which began in the 1980s as a refrigerator parts manufacturer and now owns Volvo, Lotus, Polestar and a stake in Aston Martin; and Vivo, now India’s biggest smartphone supplier.

What all have in common is that Beijing played no role in their creation. They were private companies encouraged by local governments. Huawei, BYD, and DJI emerged from Shenzhen’s Special Economic Zone, where municipal bureaucrats could write local regulations without regard for national rules. Geely was quietly supported by Zhejiang province at a time when only state-designated automakers were meant to build cars. Vivo spun off from a company founded in Dongguan, after Zhongshan, the neighboring city, wouldn’t give the company leaders equity.

Some sectors, such as batteries, electronics, and most recently electric vehicles, have received special support from Beijing as strategic industries. Companies in these areas benefited from subsidies, tax rebates, and in the case of electric cars, sales tax exemptions. But though the state was happy to lend its support to certain sectors, it was agnostic as to which specific firms and regions rose to dominance by means of that support. Beijing set a prize, and local bureaucrats competed to win it.

Hefei, the capital of Anhui province in inland Eastern China, is the most famous illustration of this process in action. In 2008, the municipal government invested $500 million in the electronic display company BOE Technology to build a new-generation LCD production line, bringing China to the cutting edge of panel production for the first time. At the time, Hefei was an unremarkable city with no display industry, and BOE was only the world’s ninth-largest manufacturer of LCD displays. The city provided the necessary land, utility connections, and cheap capital (investing almost a tenth of its total revenue that year) to set up a subsidiary company with BOE, in which it had an 81 percent stake. The bet paid off. BOE is now the world’s largest display panel manufacturer and makes about a quarter of smartphone screens worldwide.

The city reinvested the returns from its investment in other venture capital–like bets, which have won big surprisingly often. Hefei’s investment in carmaker NIO, which the city backed in 2020 in exchange for a 24 percent stake, paid off with an internal rate of return exceeding 30 percent. CXMT (Changxin Memory Technologies), 24 percent of which is directly or indirectly owned by the city of Hefei, runs just behind Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron with 7 percent of the global market for DRAM chips, the short-term memory used in smartphones, PCs, and data centers. Over the decade to 2023, the city had invested roughly $25 billion of public funds, generating reported earnings of nearly $9 billion.…

item.title: Victorian elites stayed in bed until the afternoon
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, interesting historical perspective

This is our third article from Issue 26, which arrives with print subscribers this week.

Books about successful people often make success sound rather unappealing. Education should be intense and rigorous, focused on driving up IQ and on the ‘STEM’ quaternity of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. Once adulthood is reached, life follows an austere pattern, with a 5am start, cold baths, daily visits to the gym, little or no alcohol, a Huel-rich diet, and Stakhanovite working hours. This last point generates particular excitement, and descriptions of powerful people dwell with eager fascination on how many hours they devote to their labors.

The elites of Victorian Britain operated differently. Their schools and universities were not terribly academic and had very little STEM. As adults, they got up late, drank a lot, and spent a remarkable share of their waking hours partying. They loved feasting, sports, holidays, dancing, and dressing up. Contrary to their stodgy reputation, they were probably a lot of fun.

Despite this, the elites of nineteenth-century Britain were, by their own lights, extremely successful. For much of the century, Britain was the richest country on Earth. Its companies dominated global commerce, industry and finance. Its huge navy reigned over the world’s oceans, and its tiny army won a long sequence of wars while keeping watch over an enormous empire. Britain progressed gradually toward democracy with none of the revolutions and civil wars that wracked continental Europe. There is a longstanding view that the prosperity of Britain’s elites came at the cost of the hundreds of millions whom they subordinated and oppressed, and no doubt that is at least partly true. But on their own terms, the British ruling class enjoyed a victorious century.

Maybe the Victorian elite succeeded in spite of being feckless and incompetent: the Industrial Revolution created great wealth, which they enjoyed passively and parasitically. We cannot run controlled experiments on Victorian Britain, so this thesis is hard to test. But I want to explore the possibility that a relentless focus on soft skills, team building, and intra-elite networking actually worked rather well. Huel, STEM, and cold baths have their merits. But the example of the Victorians should make us hesitate before concluding that there is only one way to rule the world.

School

Caricaturing a little, we can distinguish two groups in modern educational debates: traditionalists and progressives. Traditionalists think that education should prioritize acquiring knowledge, that it should focus on ‘hard’ subjects like science, mathematics, and foreign languages, and that it should take place in a highly structured environment, where students’ time and behavior are tightly regulated. Progressives think that education should prioritize acquiring skills, that it should embrace ‘soft’ subjects beyond the supposed academic core, and that students should be given wide freedom in which to develop personally and socially.

One might assume that Victorian education was at the extreme traditionalist end of the spectrum, and modern educational progressives would indeed be horrified by the rote learning and corporal punishment of Victorian schooling. But in respect of all the controversies listed above, elite Victorian schools lean curiously toward the ‘progressive’ side of the spectrum.

Most socially elite Victorian boys began formal education at the age of seven or eight, spending about five years in a ‘preparatory school’ before passing on to a ‘public school’ (which, to the enduring confusion of international observers, is a kind of elite private school). There was a hierarchy of public schools, with the nine ‘Clarendon schools’ at the top, and just one, Eton College, clearly at the apex. About 30 percent of nineteenth-century cabinet ministers and 40 percent of prime ministers were Old Etonians.

Most students at both preparatory and public schools were boarders, meaning that elite Victorians were generally sent away from home by the age of eight and spent their childhoods more with peers than with family. In this respect they were distinctive even in their own time: elite families in continental Europe and the United States were far more likely to keep their children at home and educate them at small local private schools. It is plausible that this contributed to the lack of subnational loyalties in the British elite, in contrast to the distinct elites of, for example, the Southern United States, Catalonia in Spain, or Hungary in the Austrian Empire.

The public schools were of course single-sex, generating a somewhat febrile atmosphere in which intense quasi-romantic (or sometimes actually romantic) relationships between boys were common. Perhaps the powerful ties of nostalgia and loyalty that students felt for their former schoolmates were linked to this. The writer Jan Morris said that ‘the whole of English upper-class life…was shot through with bisexual instinct’ and that ‘the public school system…meant that male relationships were full of emotional nuance and undertone’. Demonstrative affection remained normal in adult life, and it was completely standard for pairs of Victorian men to walk arm-in-arm in public.…
